### Four ways to send someone to the shops

Module 1 gave you the loop: think, act, observe, repeat. That is the engine. This page is about
the **shapes** you can build with it — because "an agent" is not one thing, and choosing the wrong
shape is how teams lose a month.

Send four different people to buy ingredients for dinner and watch what they do.

**The first person improvises.** They walk in, look around, think *"no basil — I'll use
parsley"*, pick it up, think again, move on. One thought, one action, one look at the result, over
and over. Flexible, and you cannot predict what they will come back with.

**The second person plans first.** They stand at the door and write the full list: aisle 3, aisle
7, checkout. Then they execute it without re-thinking. Fast and predictable — and if the shop has
moved aisle 7, the plan fails and they do not notice.

**The third person checks their own work.** They shop, then stop at the door and re-read the list
against the basket. Missing the garlic. They go back. Slower, and noticeably more likely to come
home with everything.

**The fourth is a team.** One person fetches vegetables, another the meat, a third checks the
budget. Faster in principle — and every handover is a chance to bring back the wrong thing (Module
2 of Week 32 measured exactly that cost).

Those four are the real agent architectures, and each has a name in this field.

### The first one has a name you will hear constantly: ReAct

The improviser — think, act, observe, repeat — is called **ReAct**, from a 2022 paper whose title
says the whole idea: *reasoning and acting*, interleaved. Before ReAct, systems either reasoned
(wrote out a plan and never touched the world) or acted (called tools with no thinking in
between). ReAct's contribution was to alternate them, so the thinking can *use what the last
action returned*.

In the transcript it looks exactly like this, and you can read it like a diary:

```text
Thought: I need last month's revenue for the Berlin store.
Action:  run_sql("select sum(total) from orders where city='Berlin' and month='2026-08'")
Observation: 184,220

Thought: The user asked for the change versus July. I need July too.
Action:  run_sql("select sum(total) from orders where city='Berlin' and month='2026-07'")
Observation: 201,540

Thought: Down 8.6%. I have what I need.
Answer:  Berlin revenue fell 8.6% in August, from €201,540 to €184,220.
```

Three things are worth noticing, because they are the whole architecture:

- The **thought** is written *out loud, into the transcript* — which means the next step can use
  it. Same mechanism as Week 25 Module 5: the model can only use what has been written.
- The **observation** is not the model's opinion. It is the real result of your code running a
  real query. This is where the agent touches reality.
- The loop ends when the model stops asking for tools and answers instead.

### The other three, briefly

**Plan-then-execute.** Ask for a full plan first, then run the steps. Cheaper and far more
predictable than ReAct — every step is known before anything happens, so you can show it to a
human for approval. The weakness is rigidity: a plan made before step 1 cannot know what step 4
discovered.

**Reflection.** After producing an answer, the agent critiques its own work against the goal and
tries again if it falls short. Reliably improves quality; reliably multiplies cost, because every
attempt is paid for. Reserve it for jobs where being wrong is expensive.

**Multi-agent.** Several specialised agents with an orchestrator (Week 32 Module 2). The
temptation is to reach for this first because it feels like building a company. Reach for it last.

### The part nobody puts in the diagram: the harness

Here is what actually separates an agent that survives Monday from one that does not, and it is
none of the above.

Around whichever architecture you pick, there is a layer of ordinary, unglamorous code — the
**harness** — and it does all the work the architecture diagram ignores:

- it builds the prompt each turn and decides what history to keep (Module 3);
- it validates every tool argument before executing anything (Module 2);
- it catches the tool that threw, and hands the model a *useful error* instead of crashing;
- it counts turns, tiles and money, and stops the run when a budget is spent (Week 32 M4);
- it records every step so you can see what happened afterwards (Week 34 M1);
- it decides what to do when the model asks for a tool that does not exist, or asks for the same
  one nine times in a row.

Frameworks are, almost entirely, other people's harnesses. That is the honest way to read the
landscape: they differ far less in "which architecture" than in *how much harness they give you
and how much control they take away*.

### The frameworks, honestly

You will meet these names in every job advert. Here is what each actually is:

| Framework | The shape it prefers | Reach for it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **LangGraph** | An explicit graph of steps, with state | You want production control: audit trails, resume points, human approval gates |
| **OpenAI Agents SDK** | A model-driven loop with handoffs | You want something small and standard; it works with many providers, not only OpenAI |
| **CrewAI** | Role-playing agents in a "crew" | The team metaphor genuinely fits your problem and you want to move fast |
| **AutoGen** *(Microsoft)* | Conversational multi-agent | Research-flavoured multi-agent conversation is the point |
| **smolagents** *(Hugging Face)* | The model writes **Python code** instead of JSON tool calls | Small single-agent scripts; you want to read every line it ran |
| **Pydantic AI** | A typed, tested loop (Module 5) | You want the agent to look like ordinary production software |

Two honest observations. First, **you already built the core of all of them** in Module 1 — forty
lines, no framework. Second, the correct first question is not *"which framework?"* but *"is this
a workflow or an agent?"* (Module 1). A fixed sequence of steps written in plain code beats every
framework on this list, when the steps are known.

<Check>
**The answer to the opening question, plainly.** An agent's architecture is **the shape of its
loop**: ReAct interleaves a written-out thought, a real action and a real observation, so each
step can use what the last one returned; plan-then-execute decides everything up front and gains
predictability while losing adaptability; reflection re-checks its own work at multiplied cost;
multi-agent splits the job and pays for every handover. And what actually decides whether it
survives production is not the architecture at all but the **harness** — the validation, budgets,
error handling and tracing wrapped around it, which is most of what a framework is selling you.
</Check>

<Accordion title="Checkpoint — 6 questions before you continue">
1. **What does ReAct interleave, and why does it matter?** Reasoning and acting — the thought is written into the transcript, so the next step can use what the last observation returned.
2. **Where does an observation come from?** Your code, running a real tool — not from the model. It is the agent's contact with reality.
3. **What does plan-then-execute buy and cost?** Predictability and a plan a human can approve; it cannot adapt to what a later step discovers.
4. **When is reflection worth its price?** When being wrong is more expensive than paying for a second and third attempt.
5. **What is the harness?** The ordinary code around the loop: prompt building, validation, error handling, budgets, and tracing.
6. **What is the first question to ask before choosing a framework?** Whether the problem is a workflow (fixed steps → plain code) or genuinely an agent.
</Accordion>

You now know the shapes, and that most of the reliability lives in the harness rather than the
architecture. One agent, however well built, is still one worker doing one thing at a time.

Real work has branches that could run at once, steps that must not repeat, and jobs long enough
that something *will* fail halfway through. Coordinating that — and surviving it — is

  <Tab title="🔵 Layer 2 — Build">
    **You ship code for a living?** This layer is yours — trade-offs, real tools, real versions.

    A prototype agent works on the demo query and loops forever on the second one. The difference
    between those two outcomes is almost never the architecture — it is the twenty lines of harness
    nobody wrote.

### Writing the harness yourself

Before adopting a framework, write this once. It is short, and it is the thing you will otherwise
be unable to debug inside somebody else's abstraction:

```python
# harness.py — the loop from Module 1, made survivable
import json, time

def run_agent(client, model, system, user, tools, handlers,
              max_turns=8, max_tiles=40_000, deadline_s=60):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user}]
    started, tiles = time.monotonic(), 0

    for turn in range(max_turns):
        if time.monotonic() - started > deadline_s:
            return {"status": "timeout", "partial": messages}
        if tiles > max_tiles:
            return {"status": "budget_spent", "partial": messages}

        reply = client.messages.create(
            model=model, system=system, tools=tools,
            max_tokens=1024, messages=messages,
        )
        tiles += reply.usage.input_tokens + reply.usage.output_tokens
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply.content})

        calls = [b for b in reply.content if getattr(b, "type", None) == "tool_use"]
        if not calls:                                     # no tool asked for → done
            return {"status": "ok", "answer": reply.content, "turns": turn + 1}

        results = []
        for call in calls:
            handler = handlers.get(call.name)
            if handler is None:                           # hallucinated tool
                out = f"Error: no tool named {call.name}. Available: {list(handlers)}"
            else:
                try:
                    out = json.dumps(handler(**call.input))
                except Exception as exc:                  # never crash the loop
                    out = f"Error: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call.id, "content": out})
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

    return {"status": "max_turns", "partial": messages}
```

Every line that is not the loop is harness: the deadline, the tile budget, the unknown-tool case,
the exception that becomes a message instead of a crash, and the explicit statuses so the caller
knows *why* it stopped.

### The error message is part of the prompt

The most under-appreciated line above is `out = f"Error: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"`. That
string goes straight back to the model, which means **your error text is prompt engineering**.

- `"Error"` → the model tries something random.
- `"Error: order TX-4471 not found. Order ids look like AB-1234; check the id and try again."` →
  the model corrects itself on the next turn, usually first time.

Write tool errors for the reader who will act on them. That reader is a language model.

### Choosing a framework with numbers

Do this in an afternoon rather than by reading blog posts. Take one real task from your product,
implement it three times — your own harness, plus two candidate frameworks — and record: lines of
code, tiles per successful run, p95 latency, success rate over twenty real inputs, and how long it
took *you* to debug the first failure. That last column is the one that decides, and it is the one
no comparison table on the internet contains.

Practical guidance from that exercise, repeatedly:

- If the steps are knowable in advance, plain code wins on every column. Do not skip this test.
- If you need approval gates, resume-after-failure and audit trails, a graph framework
  (**LangGraph**) earns its complexity — those are exactly Week 32's requirements.
- If you want the agent to be ordinary software with types and tests, **Pydantic AI** (Module 5).
- If you want to *read* everything the agent did, **smolagents** writing Python is unusually
  legible — and unusually dangerous without a sandbox, since executing model-written code is
  exactly as risky as it sounds.

  <Tab title="🟣 Layer 3 — Edge">
    **For anyone who has shipped this and been burned.** Internals, scale, numbers.

    Agent failures are rarely a wrong answer. They are a right answer produced after nine
    unnecessary tool calls, or a loop that never ends, or a run that succeeded twice.

### Where agent loops actually fail

Four failure modes, in the order you will meet them:

1. **The repeated call.** The model asks for the same tool with the same arguments over and over,
   because the observation did not change and nothing in the transcript says "you already tried
   this". Fix in the harness: detect an identical (tool, args) pair and return
   *"You already called this and received X. Try something different or answer."*
2. **Compounding error.** Each turn has some chance of a wrong step; over eight turns those
   multiply. This is the arithmetic behind Module 1's "most problems are workflows" — fewer turns
   is not a stylistic preference, it is a reliability argument.
3. **The confident dead end.** The agent decides early that a tool is broken and works around it
   for the rest of the run. Detect it by scoring the *path* and not only the answer (Week 33 M3).
4. **Silent partial success.** Half the plan completed, the answer written as though all of it
   did. Only per-step verification catches this.

### The context that grows until it breaks

Every turn appends the model's output and the tool result, so the prompt grows monotonically. A
run with big tool outputs — a SQL result, a page of HTML — hits the context limit while looking
completely healthy, and costs rise quadratically-ish in the number of turns because each turn
re-sends everything before it.

Two mitigations that actually work: **truncate tool outputs at the harness** (return the first N
rows plus a count, never the whole table), and **summarise older turns** once you pass a threshold
(Module 3). Both are harness code; neither is provided by the architecture you chose.

### What the benchmarks do and do not tell you

Agent benchmark numbers are among the least transferable in this field. The scaffolding around the
model — the harness, the tool descriptions, the retry policy — moves scores by more than the model
choice does, which means a published comparison is measuring somebody else's harness as much as
their model. Treat leaderboard positions as a shortlist, then run **your** task on **your**
harness before believing anything.

### Papers and primary sources

- [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629) — Yao et al., 2022. Read this for the original interleaving argument and its evaluation on HotPotQA, FEVER, ALFWorld and WebShop.
- [Anthropic — Building Effective Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents). Read this for the workflow-versus-agent decision and the patterns that survive production.
- [Anthropic — tool use overview](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview). Read this for the current tool-calling shapes your harness must handle.

### Stretch challenge

Instrument your harness to record, for twenty real runs: turns used, tiles spent, repeated calls,
and whether the final answer was correct. Then implement *one* change — repeated-call detection,
or tool-output truncation, or better error messages — and re-run the same twenty. Report which
column moved. Most teams find the error-message change moves success rate more than switching
model does, and almost nobody tries it first.

## Hands-on

Take the forty-line agent from Module 1 and add the harness from Layer 2 — budgets, validation,
error messages, statuses. Then deliberately break a tool and watch whether the agent recovers.
That single exercise is the difference between a demo and something you would put on call.

## Apply it at work

**For the student.** Being able to say "this is a ReAct loop, and here is the harness around it"
in an interview puts you ahead of most candidates, who can name frameworks but not describe what
they do.

**For the professional.** Before your team adopts a framework, run the three-implementation
comparison from Layer 2. It takes an afternoon and it is the only version of that decision that
survives a design review.

## Assessment

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="6 concept questions">
  1. What does the "Re" and the "Act" in ReAct refer to? (Reasoning and acting, interleaved rather than separated.)
  2. Why must the thought be written into the transcript? (Generation is sequential; a step can only use what has already been written.)
  3. What does plan-then-execute give up in exchange for predictability? (Adaptation — the plan cannot use what a later step discovered.)
  4. Name three responsibilities of the harness. (Any of: prompt/history construction, argument validation, error handling, budgets and limits, tracing, repeated-call detection.)
  5. Why do agent benchmark results transfer poorly? (Scaffolding — harness, tool descriptions, retries — affects scores as much as the model does.)
  6. What is the first question before choosing a framework? (Is this a workflow or an agent? Fixed steps belong in plain code.)
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Coding challenge">
  Extend the Layer 2 harness with: repeated-call detection that returns a corrective observation;
  tool-output truncation with a row count; and a `trace` list recording every (thought, tool, args,
  result, tiles) tuple. Hidden tests check: an identical repeated call never executes the handler
  twice; a 10,000-row tool result never enters the message history whole; and the trace length
  equals the number of turns actually taken.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Interview questions (junior / mid / senior)">
  - **Junior:** "Describe the ReAct loop in your own words."
  - **Mid:** "Our agent occasionally calls the same tool nine times and then times out. Walk me through your diagnosis and the fix."
  - **Senior:** "We are choosing between building our own agent harness and adopting a framework, for a system with human approval gates and a resume-after-failure requirement. Make the case either way, and tell me what evidence you would gather first."
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Common mistakes

- **Choosing an architecture before asking whether it should be an agent at all.** Fixed steps belong in plain code.
- **Treating tool errors as plumbing.** They are prompts; a vague error produces a random next step.
- **Letting tool output into history unbounded.** One big SQL result can end the run.
- **Reaching for multi-agent first.** Every handover costs tiles, latency and a chance to go wrong.
- **Trusting benchmark tables.** They measure somebody else's harness as much as their model.

## Sources & further reading

**Primary docs**

- [Anthropic — tool use overview](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview). The current tool-calling contract your harness implements.
- [Anthropic — Building Effective Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents). Patterns, and the workflow-versus-agent decision.

**Go deeper**

- [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629) — Yao et al., 2022.
